findings.title: Lease term, premises and initial rent exposure
findings.interpretation: The lease runs 15 years from 1 January 2024 to 31 December 2038 for floors 8–10 of 100 Bishopsgate (32,500 sq ft). Initial rent is £850,000 p.a. exclusive of VAT. The lease is subject to upward-only rent reviews at years 5 and 10 with no stated caps or collars, and the tenant continues to pay existing rent until a new rate is determined. The tenant is also liable for ongoing service charge contributions (18.7% of building costs) as additional rent, plus VAT and building insurance reimbursement.
findings.relevance: Establishes the quantum of fixed financial commitment and identifies that rent escalation is uncapped and triggered by fixed dates. The 18.7% service charge apportionment exposes the tenant to building-wide cost inflation over 15 years. Clarification is needed on the mechanics of rent review—specifically whether the review dates align with break dates and what benchmarking methodology (open market, RPI, fixed %) applies.
findings.next_step: Obtain and review clause 3.2 (full rent review terms) and Schedule 3 (service charge composition and calculation method). Confirm whether service charge is subject to caps or exclusions. Establish the baseline rent payable at years 5 and 10 and the potential range of increases to enable financial forecasting.
findings.quote: The Term shall be for a period of fifteen (15) years commencing on 1 January 2024 and expiring on 31 December 2038, subject to earlier determination in accordance with the provisions of this Lease.
findings.uncertainty: The rent review mechanism at years 5 and 10 is not fully specified in the available pages (clause 3.2 truncated). Service charge caps, exclusions and audit rights are not yet reviewed. The impact of VAT and insurance reimbursement on total occupancy cost is not quantified.

findings.title: Upward-only rent review with expert determination and backdated interest
findings.interpretation: Rent reviews on 1 January 2029 and 1 January 2034 are upward-only, meaning rent cannot decrease. If parties cannot agree, an independent surveyor acts as expert (not arbitrator) to determine reviewed rent. If review is delayed beyond the review date, the tenant continues to pay the old rent but must pay any shortfall within 14 days of determination, plus interest at 2% above Barclays Bank base rate backdated from the review date.
findings.relevance: The absence of downward movement eliminates tenant flexibility if market rents soften. The 2% interest charge creates a backdated cost surprise if review determination is delayed. The expert determination mechanism (faster than arbitration) may favour landlord if surveyor applies an open-market approach without tenant input on valuation assumptions.
findings.next_step: Clarify the full terms of clause 3.2 (basis of review—open market rent, RPI uplift, or fixed percentage). Establish whether the surveyor's determination is binding on both parties and whether the tenant can challenge methodology. Review insurance for backdated interest liability and consider cash-flow timing risk.
findings.quote: In default of agreement between the Landlord and the Tenant as to the Reviewed Rent by the relevant Review Date, the Reviewed Rent shall be determined by an independent surveyor acting as an expert (and not as an arbitrator) appointed by agreement between the parties or, in default of agreement, by the President for the time being of the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors on the application of either party. The rent review shall be upward only.
findings.uncertainty: The basis of the reviewed rent (open market, RPI, fixed increase) is not stated in the extract. Whether the tenant has input into or can challenge the expert's valuation methodology is unclear. The interest rate (2% above Barclays base) and backdated liability calculation are confirmed, but the trigger for delayed determination and any caps on interest are not specified.

findings.title: Tenant repairing obligations: full interior and surfaces; landlord bears structure and M&E
findings.interpretation: The tenant must keep the entire premises and all interior surfaces, doors, windows and frames in good repair throughout the term, with redecoration every 5 years and in the final year. 'Fair wear and tear' is excepted. The schedule of condition (Schedule 4) limits the tenant's obligation to not put the premises in better condition than at commencement. The landlord is responsible for the building structure, exterior walls, roof, foundations, lifts, air conditioning, fire systems and common area lighting; landlord's costs are recovered from the tenant as part of service charge (18.7% share).
findings.relevance: The tenant bears full liability for interior decoration and M&E maintenance throughout the 15-year term, creating an ongoing cost exposure. The 'fair wear and tear' exception provides some protection but is fact-dependent and often contested. The schedule of condition is a key protective mechanism. However, the tenant's 18.7% share of landlord's building costs (structure, roof, lifts, fire systems) exposes the tenant to major capital expenditure if the landlord chooses to refurbish or replace common systems. No rent abatement or cap on service charge is mentioned.
findings.next_step: Obtain and review Schedule 4 (schedule of condition) in detail to confirm baseline state and verify that all defects at commencement are recorded. Request clarification on whether tenant's repairing obligations extend to any structural or shared M&E (e.g., pipes serving the premises). Confirm service charge exclusions and whether the landlord can recover 100% of capital expenditure or if there is a cap or apportionment by age/benefit. Establish whether the 18.7% share is fixed or variable by floor or use.
findings.quote: The Tenant shall keep the Premises and every part thereof (including all additions and alterations thereto) in good and substantial repair and condition throughout the Term, fair wear and tear excepted, and shall yield up the Premises in such repair and condition at the expiration or sooner determination of the Term.
findings.uncertainty: The scope of 'good and substantial repair' is not defined. Whether the tenant's obligations extend to internal structural elements (e.g., load-bearing columns, floors) shared with other tenants is unclear. The service charge calculation and any exclusions or recovery caps are not detailed in the reviewed pages. Whether Schedule 4 fully captures the premises' condition and protects the tenant against disputes over 'fair wear and tear' depends on its completeness—not yet verified.

findings.title: Break clauses at years 5 and 10 with 12-month notice and conditions TBD
findings.interpretation: The tenant may determine the lease on 1 January 2029 (year 5) or 1 January 2034 (year 10) by serving 12 months' prior written notice under Section 196 Law of Property Act 1925. Once notice is given it is irrevocable. Conditions for exercise are stated to be in clause 8.3.1, but the clause text is incomplete in the search results.
findings.relevance: The tenant has two opportunities to exit the lease after 5 and 10 years respectively, providing business flexibility. However, the 12-month notice requirement means the tenant must commit to exit by year 4 or year 9 respectively—a significant planning constraint. The conditions precedent to exercise (clause 8.3.1) are not yet reviewed and may impose strict requirements (e.g., repair obligations satisfied, no rent arrears, tenant not in default) that could trap the tenant if conditions cannot be met.
findings.next_step: Obtain full text of clause 8.3 to confirm conditions for break exercise, including repair obligations, rent/service charge arrears, breach status and any indemnity requirements. Verify that conditions are objective and within the tenant's control, and establish whether the landlord can refuse the break if conditions are not satisfied. Assess whether the 12-month notice period creates cash-flow or operational pressure if the tenant needs to vacate at short notice.
findings.quote: The Tenant may determine this Lease on the fifth (5th) anniversary of the Term Commencement Date (being 1 January 2029) or the tenth (10th) anniversary of the Term Commencement Date (being 1 January 2034) (each a "Break Date") by serving written notice on the Landlord in accordance with clause 8.2.
findings.uncertainty: The conditions precedent to break exercise (clause 8.3.1) are not fully disclosed. Whether the tenant must satisfy repair obligations, be up-to-date with rent/service charge, and not be in material breach is unknown. Whether the landlord can refuse or delay the break if conditions are not satisfied is unclear. Whether any premium or reinstatement obligation applies on break is not stated.

findings.title: Landlord's insurance obligation; tenant reimburses 18.7% of premiums and excess as additional rent
findings.interpretation: The landlord insures the building (including premises) against defined insured risks (fire, flood, storm, subsidence, etc.) for full reinstatement value including professional fees, demolition and VAT, and loss of rent for 3+ years. The landlord uses reasonable endeavours to obtain a subrogation waiver from the insurer against the tenant. The tenant reimburses to the landlord a 'fair proportion' (being 18.7%, matching the service charge share) of premiums and any policy excess. Such reimbursement is treated as additional rent.
findings.relevance: The tenant's insurance cost is variable and not capped—if building insurance premiums rise (e.g., due to building age, location, flood risk or insurer market conditions), the tenant's share rises proportionately. The landlord's subrogation waiver protects the tenant from the insurer pursuing it for claims, but only to the extent the waiver is obtained. The 18.7% share is fixed to the premises' proportion of lettable area; it does not adjust if other parts of the building become vacant or the landlord's insurance costs change materially.
findings.next_step: Obtain a copy of the landlord's current building insurance policy and schedule of premiums to establish baseline cost. Verify that the subrogation waiver has been secured and review its scope (does it cover all insured risks and negligence scenarios?). Confirm whether the policy excess is reasonable and who bears excess costs if a claim arises. Establish whether the tenant can request competitive quotes or audit the landlord's insurance procurement.
findings.quote: The Tenant shall reimburse to the Landlord on demand a fair proportion (being the Tenant's proportion as defined in clause 4.2.3) of the premium paid or payable by the Landlord for such insurance and any excess applicable under the policy. Such reimbursement shall constitute additional rent payable under this Lease.
findings.uncertainty: The scope and adequacy of the landlord's insurance cover are not verified—specific risks excluded or sub-limits applied may leave gaps. The status of the subrogation waiver negotiation is unknown. Whether the excess amount is reasonable, who covers it on claim, and whether the tenant can negotiate a lower excess are not addressed. The basis for apportioning 'fair proportion' as 18.7% is not explained (whether it is lettable area, occupied area, or a fixed percentage).

findings.title: Broad environmental indemnity from tenant covering contamination and statutory liability
findings.interpretation: The tenant indemnifies the landlord against all claims, costs and liabilities arising from environmental contamination or damage caused by the tenant's acts, omissions or operations at the premises. The indemnity extends to statutory liability under Part IIA Environmental Protection Act 1990, Water Resources Act 1991 and other environmental legislation. The indemnity has no temporal or financial limit stated.
findings.relevance: This is a strict-liability indemnity with no causation threshold (does not require negligence or breach of duty). It captures liability for historical contamination discovered during the term, pollution from the tenant's operations, and statutory cleanup costs imposed on the landlord. The absence of caps or exclusions (e.g., for pre-existing contamination, landlord negligence or building defects) means the tenant bears potentially unlimited environmental liability. This is particularly onerous for a financial services tenant using standard office operations.
findings.next_step: Request clarification from the landlord on whether the environmental indemnity extends to pre-existing contamination and whether it is limited to contamination caused solely by the tenant's operations (excluding neighbouring tenants, the landlord or building services). Obtain an environmental Phase 1 survey of the premises and building to identify baseline contamination risk. Establish whether the tenant's professional indemnity or pollution liability insurance covers this indemnity and obtain quotes. Negotiate exclusions for pre-existing conditions and landlord negligence.
findings.quote: The Tenant shall indemnify and keep indemnified the Landlord against all claims, costs and liabilities arising from or in connection with any contamination of or damage to the environment (including the Premises, the Building, the air, soil, groundwater, surface water and any living organism) caused by or attributable to the acts, omissions or operations of the Tenant or any person at the Premises with the express or implied authority of the Tenant.
findings.uncertainty: Whether the indemnity applies to pre-existing contamination, contamination by other tenants or building service providers, and the landlord's own negligence is unclear. Whether 'caused by or attributable to' requires direct causation or extends to remote or contributory causes is a matter of interpretation. Whether the tenant's insurance policies cover this broad indemnity is unknown. The lease does not state whether the indemnity survives termination or applies only during the term.
